newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African army officers named in activist murders.
newsitem.headline: S.African army officers named in activist murders.

text.p: A South African apartheid-era police brigadier implicated several senior army officers in the murder of black activists on Wednesday, continuing the pattern of former officials turning in others.

Brigadier Jack Cronje, who earlier blamed apartheid atrocities on former political leaders -- including ex-president P.W. Botha -- said the South African Defence Force killed Fabian Ribeiro and his wife Florence in 1986.

Ribeiro, fondly known as the "peoples' doctor" but accused by police of recruiting activists for the armed wing of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, was killed by a volley of shots into the couple's home outside Pretoria.

In his amnesty application for the 27 murders Cronje is accused of committing as commander of a secret police death squad, he said a member of the Civil Cooperation Bureau (CCB), the army's hit-squad component, asked him to prepare a file on Ribeiro.

"I later heard that Ribeiro and his wife were shot by two black men under the command...of the special forces," Cronje told the Amnesty Committee of Nobel laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
The commission hopes ex-officials implicated by their colleagues will in turn name more names.
Cronje said that after the high-profile murder, the commanders of the Special Forces and of the CCB asked him to derail a police investigation into the killings.

In its submission to the truth commission last week, the Defence Force failed to accept any blame for human rights abuses. Commission deputy chairman Alex Boraine termed the submission "breathtakingly one-sided".

Former state assassin Eugene de Kock, jailed for 212 years on Wednesday by a criminal court for apartheid murders, also fingered senior police and government officials recently in testimony aimed at reducing the severity of his sentences.
Tutu told Reuters at the amnesty hearings on Wednesday that while de Kock's sentence was fitting, those who gave him his orders also had to be called to account.

"He was part of a whole system and there were those who gave orders. Those who were ultimately responsible must not be allowed to get away...The foot soldiers must not be the only ones who get clobbered," he said.
